newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian analysts see December qtr rate cut.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian analysts see December qtr rate cut.

text.p: The next move in Australian official interest rates is likely to be a cut, following July's first cut in three years, and it is likely to happen in the last quarter of 1996, economists say.
But if there is no cut by the end of the year, the next move in rates could be a rise in mid 1997 when the economy is likely to be picking up steam, they said.

"On a 'balance of probabilities' approach, as distinct from 'beyond reasonable doubt', the next move in monetary policy looks to be an easing," Citibank Australia economists said in a report. "But only just," they added.

Of the 35 economists Reuters surveyed ahead of Tuesday's Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board meeting, the first since rates were lowered by 0.5 percent to 7.00 percent, only one saw a September change as a possibility.
The July 31 cut in official rates caught many by surprise.
Economists said there has not been any real new information released since then to justify another cut.
Although the June quarter GDP data released in August showed a flat economy, that would have been factored into the July decision, they said.

"Not only would another move in such a short space of time, in such a relatively low interest rate environment, be unprecedented, the data released since the last move do not provide a justification for another easing so soon after the last one," Commonwealth bank economist Tim Moloney said.

However, while September is not expected to yield a change, the December quarter is. Of the 35 surveyed, 24 economists believe that rates will fall in the fourth quarter, with many citing November as the most likely time for the cut.
"I think that a cut in November/December is much more likley," Rothschild Australia chief economist Ric Simes said.
"November would be on the back of again benign numbers on the inflation front and wages, or December on the back of a subdued GDP number for the September quarter," he said.
Even then, good inflation and wages numbers would not be enought to justify a cut on their own. The key would be whether the weakness in the labour market continued, economists said.

A moderating inflation and wages outlook into the end of 1996, with perhaps some uncertainty over wages into 1997, should already be factored into the RBA's thinking, and economists said this did appear to fit with recent pronouncements from the bank.

"There's no need to (cut), I don't think the economy's going to be looking recessionary," Bain and Co economist Tony Meer said. "(But) if you continue to get sluggish employment numbers and good inflation numbers, then why not?"

However, if the U.S. were to raise interest rates before the end of the year, it could rule out a local rate cut because of the pressure, and possible resultant inflationary effects, a cut would place on the Australian dollar.
"If there's a rise in the U.S. it puts a bit of pressure on them not to move," ABN Amro economist Susan Creighton said.
And just as there were good reasons for a cut, economist said a case could also be made leaving rates unchanged and then lifting them in mid 1997.

Economists said the government's outlook for the economy to pick up through 1996/97 (July/June), backed up by strong capital expenditure surveys, meant that if rates were cut again the RBA would be reacting to current weakness rather than being forward looking in allowing for the lags in monetary policy.
With the outlook for wages is uncertain into 1997, a cut now could fuel inflation just when the economy begins to pick up in 1997, they said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
